Armstrong Family Archive · Bellville / Austin County, Texas
Community Reconstruction · Primary Sources · Bellville, Texas

John Nichols and the Community After Emancipation

A documentary reconstruction of the Nichols enslavement record, the nine unnamed people recorded in 1860, the family clusters that emerge after emancipation, and the land and heir network that kept the Nichols name in Bellville for generations.

Austin County · Texas 1860 Slave Schedule Family Clusters Land & Heirs
01 / FRAME
The question is no longer “Who was Easter?”
The page now starts with the documented population and lets the family connections emerge from the records.

When an early settler appears in the records as both a landholder and an enslaver, African American genealogy cannot stop at the enslaver's name. The researcher has to reconstruct the household, the people held there, the land, the children and heirs of the enslaver, the people who lived nearby, and the families who carried the Nichols name after emancipation.

This page therefore follows the Nichols community and descendant network. The nine people in the 1860 John Nichols slave schedule remain the documentary population baseline. The later Black Nichols families are then studied as possible descendant, kinship, property, and community clusters.

Working historical proposition

Because John Nichols was an early Bellville-area settler with a documented enslaved population, the appearance of Black families using the Nichols name in the same community is treated as a serious descendant/community research signal. The working question is whether those families descend from people enslaved by John Nichols, by his children, or through closely connected Nichols kin and property networks. A surname is a lead; the individual relationship still has to be reconstructed from records.

Documented

The Nichols population

John Nichols enslaved people in Tennessee and later Texas; the 1860 Austin County schedule records nine unnamed people.

Being reconstructed

The family clusters

Post-emancipation Nichols households, marriages, children, voter registrations, land interests, and later heirs.

Not assumed

One giant family

Rendy/Easter, Patience/Clarissa, Joseph's family, and the nine 1860 entries remain separate until a documentary bridge connects them.

02 / NICHOLS
John Nichols before and in Texas
The strongest context for the 1860 population comes from Nichols's earlier enslaving history.

John Nichols was born in Louisiana ca. 1797, as reflected in the 1860 Austin County free population census. Before Texas he was documented in Williamson County, Tennessee, from at least 1828 through 1835.

In 1828 he purchased an enslaved woman named Harriet at public auction for $306 (Nichols vs. Hardeman and West, Williamson County Chancery Court, December 23, 1829). By 1830 the federal slave schedule records 24 enslaved people in his Williamson County household.

In 1832 Benjamin W. Bedford obtained a legal attachment against Milley, Harriet, and Harriet's infant daughter Fanny. Nichols refused to surrender them. The sheriff's 1835 return was marked Not Found. The court record is consistent with Nichols having left Tennessee for Texas with the people sought under the attachment (Bedford vs. Nichols, Williamson County Chancery Court, 1832–1835, FamilySearch Image Group 008479344).

The Stephen F. Austin Register of Families, Page 80, records John Nicholls, age 33, wife Fanny age 31, two children, and one other dependent, farmer, origin Sabine, arrival 1827. The record does not name that dependent or state the person's status. The broader Nichols record establishes that Nichols was enslaving people; therefore the unnamed dependent is an important enslavement-network lead, but the person's identity remains unknown.

John Nichols received one league and one labor of land from the Mexican government on October 20, 1832. He later sold portions to James and Thomas Bell. The 1837–1866 Austin County deed books and 1825–1835 Spanish deeds remain active research targets for reconstructing land and possible enslaved-person transfers.

03 / CLUSTERS
Build the people into family clusters
These groups are deliberately kept separate. The research question is where, and whether, the records eventually make them intersect.

Patience → Clarissa → Amanda / Harriet

Documented property-family cluster

The Waldrop/Davenport records place Patience and her descendants within a South Carolina–Mississippi property network. The 1839 Rankin County, Mississippi deed (Deed Book 4, Page 435) names Fanny Micholes/Fanny Waldrop Nichols among the eight children appearing jointly as grantees while reciting Patience and her increase; it does not establish a person-specific allocation to Fanny. The record is important for reconstructing Patience's descendants and the movement of enslaved property through the Waldrop family. It does not by itself identify Rendy or Easter as members of the John Nichols 1860 population.

Patience · mother/grandmother clusterClarissa · documented descendantAmanda · Clarissa's childHarriet · Clarissa's child

Rendy Blayn → Easter Bell

Separate identity cluster

Easter's 1935 death certificate identifies her mother as Rendy Blayn/Bland (the original record wording is retained as the source form). Easter's later census, marriage, death, and property records establish a substantial Bellville life story. The Rendy/Easter connection is real research; their placement inside John Nichols's 1860 schedule is not currently established.

Joseph Nichols household

Post-emancipation Bellville cluster

Joseph Nichols married Easter Bell after emancipation. The post-emancipation record places Joseph and Easter with children including Allen, Josephine, Oscar, and Clara. Henry Nichols appears immediately adjacent to Joseph and Easter in the 1880 Precinct 1 census; the proximity is a useful family/community lead, while the exact relationship remains a reconstruction question.

Later Nichols descendants & heirs

Community / property network

The later Bellville Nichols network includes Allen/Diana/Dora, Oscar/Clara Alexander, Henry/Emiline/Delia, Anna/William King, Josephine/Louis Biggs Pink, Willie/Delphia Lilly, and Helen/Hellen Nichols Armstrong. These are retained because they help reconstruct the post-emancipation community, not because every person has yet been assigned to one of the nine 1860 entries.

05 / JOSEPH
Could one of the two mulatto males be Joseph?
This is a legitimate hypothesis question—not a forced identification.
Candidate A

Age 22 · born ~1838

The schedule's third entry is a mulatto male age 22. That would place his birth around 1838. Later Joseph records place him in the same Bellville community, but the age is somewhat older than the later estimate. This remains possible but requires a bridge.

Candidate B

Age 18 · born ~1842

The fourth entry is a mulatto male age 18, placing his birth around 1842. This is the closer demographic match to Joseph's known/estimated birth information and therefore deserves focused record searching. It is still only a hypothesis.

What would strengthen the hypothesis?

A record naming Joseph's parent(s), an emancipation-era document, Freedmen's Bureau record, labor contract, marriage record with age/origin information, deed, probate record, or other primary source that places Joseph in the Nichols household before emancipation. The 1860 schedule alone cannot provide that bridge.

06 / WALDROP
Fanny Waldrop and the property network
This is a major contextual network, but it is not a shortcut for assigning people to the 1860 schedule.

John Nichols's wife was Frances Fanny Waldrop, daughter of Hezekiah Waldrop. Fanny was born in South Carolina ca. 1802 according to the 1860 Austin County free population census, while the 1870 census gives Tennessee; the discrepancy remains noted.

Fanny married John Nichols on October 14, 1837 in Austin County. The 1839 Rankin County, Mississippi deed, Deed Book 4 Page 435, names Fanny Micholes/Fanny Waldrop Nichols among the eight children appearing jointly as grantees while reciting Patience and her increase; it does not establish a person-specific allocation to Fanny. That deed is a critical property record for reconstructing the Patience/Clarissa cluster and the movement of enslaved property through the Waldrop family.

The broader research trail runs through South Carolina, Mississippi, and Texas. Earlier records include Davenport–Waldrop intersections, including the enslaved-property network surrounding Patience and Clarissa. These records are retained because they may eventually explain how the family clusters intersect; they are not being used to assign Rendy or Easter to John Nichols without a direct bridge.

Important distinction

The Waldrop property network and the John Nichols household overlap through Fanny, land, migration, and later community history. That overlap is research context. It is not itself proof that every person appearing in the Waldrop records later belonged to the John Nichols household.

07 / BELLVILLE
The Nichols name after emancipation
This is where the page moves from an enslaved household to a living Black community—and where the later records give us hypotheses about who those unnamed people became.

Joseph Nichols registered to vote in Bellville, Austin County, on January 27, 1868. James W. Nichols registered the following day, January 28. These Reconstruction-era voter registrations are primary-source evidence of Black men using the Nichols name in Bellville shortly after emancipation.

Henry Nichols appears immediately adjacent to Joseph and Easter in the 1880 Precinct 1 census. Henry was born ca. 1839 in Texas. Austin County marriage records document Henry Nichols and Delia Manning on December 28, 1865, and Henry Nichols and Emeline Georgia on January 23, 1879. The adjacency of Henry and Joseph is a meaningful community/family lead, while the precise relationship remains to be reconstructed.

Emeline Nickols · A possible link to the 1860 population

In 1930—65 years after emancipation—an 83-year-old Black woman named Emeline Nickols was living in Bellville, Austin County, Texas. She owned her home, valued at $300. She worked as a laundress and could not read or write. Her granddaughter, Zelma Whitmere, age 15, lived with her. The census places Emeline's birth around 1847 in Texas and reports both parents born in Texas.

The 1860 John Nichols slave schedule contains an unnamed Black female age 11, approximately born 1849. That is an age correspondence within the range expected from census-age reporting and rounding. It is therefore a legitimate identity hypothesis: Emeline could be the girl represented by that 1860 entry. It is not a confirmed identification.

If that hypothesis proves correct, Emeline would have been approximately 11 in 1860 and about 16 at emancipation. Her later use of the Nichols/Nickols surname, her long residence in Bellville, her Texas-born parents, and the existence of an unnamed Nichols “dependent” in the 1827 Austin register create a compelling cluster of research questions. The records currently do not prove that the 1827 dependent was Emeline's mother, or that Emeline was freed from John Nichols specifically. Those possibilities remain open for documentary testing.

What can be said now is that Emeline provides one of the most useful post-emancipation identity leads for the unnamed women in the 1860 Nichols population. Her 1930 census record and 1932 death record should be searched alongside marriage, land, voter, probate, Freedmen's Bureau, and neighboring household records.

08 / LAND PAPERWORK
John Nichols · 1832 Mexican-Era Land Paperwork
The land itself is part of the evidence. This four-page primary-source document is preserved here as a document image rather than reduced to a later summary.

The Armstrong Family Archive now preserves the uploaded four-page John Nichols land document as a primary-source exhibit. The first page bears the date Villa de Austin, October 20, 1832 and the signature/mark of John Nichols. The document is written in Spanish-era legal script and includes subsequent endorsements and attestations on the following pages.

This paperwork belongs at the center of the Nichols reconstruction because the later Black Nichols community is not being studied only through census households. Land is another documentary path through the generations. The Nichols Survey, later fractional interests, deeds, heirs, and the 2006 foreclosure can be followed as a property chain that may preserve relationships even where enslaved people's names disappear from the antebellum record.

The 1832 grant context already established in this archive places John Nichols on the land before the 1860 slave schedule. The research question is now broader than identifying a single enslaved person: how did the original Nichols landholding divide, who received or acquired pieces of it, and which formerly enslaved families and descendants later held legal interests?

Primary-source exhibit · uploaded document

The images below are the actual four pages supplied for this research. Page 1 visibly carries the Mexican-era heading Sello Tercero: Dos Reales, the date Villa de Austin, October 20, 1832, and the John Nichols signature/mark. Pages 2–4 continue the legal record with additional writing, endorsements, and signatures. Because the handwriting is difficult in places, the archive should not silently manufacture a full transcription from uncertain readings.

Source: uploaded four-page John Nichols land document, file 1028651.pdf · pages 1–4.
09 / LAND
The land outlived the original household
Later deeds and tax foreclosure records allow the community to be followed through property even when earlier personal records disappear.

At peak, John Nichols held approximately 4,000 acres in Austin County: 300 acres from the Stephenson grant and 3,700 acres from the Stephen F. Austin and John Hodge colonial grant, along with Bellville and Hempstead town lots. Tax records also list five horses, 75 cattle, and poll tax. J.G. Bell later acquired 240 acres from the original Nichols grant; tax records identify the original grantee as Nichols, John.

John Nichols signed documents with an X mark; Fanny also signed with a mark. John died March 3, 1864, one year before emancipation. His children were Ellen, Sarah Jane, James William, Frances Elizabeth, Samuel Houston, and Caroline Mary.

The 1876 pension records show Fanny in Travis County in indigent circumstances. She received $37.50 per quarter as the widow of Texas Revolution soldier John Nichols, with witnesses James B. Pier, Nathaniel Reed, and S.G. Reams confirming his service. By 1877 Sam H. Nichols was in Travis County managing her affairs; by 1879 James W. Nichols was writing from Coleman County. John W. Nichols later purchased 100 acres in Coleman County in 1891 for $650, paid off by 1903.

Texas Revolution · 1836

John Nichols / Jack Nichols

Served in Captain R.H. McNutt's Company. Witnesses later confirmed his service and his furnishing cattle to the Texas Army.

10 / HEIRS
The 2006 property network
A later court record provides a map of the descendants and heirs attached to the Nichols Survey property.

In 2006 Austin County filed a tax foreclosure suit, Cause No. 97V-003, in the 155th Judicial District Court. The property sold at foreclosure on August 1, 2006 and was recorded November 1, 2006. The chain traces to the John Nichols Survey, Abstract No. 73, including a fractional two-acre tract associated with Volume 209, Page 228 of the Austin County Deed Records.

The named defendants/legal heirs included Easter Pink (Easter Bell Nichols), Allen Nichols, Oscar Nichols, Clara Nazy (Clara Nichols Nagy), Joseph King, Charley King, Annie King (Annie Nichols King), Helen Armstrong a.k.a. Helen Gilbert (Hellen Nichols Armstrong), Joseph Nichols, Willey Nichols, and Myrtle T. Everline.

This record is important because it demonstrates a later Nichols property/heir network. It should not be read backward as proof that every named heir descended from a particular person in the 1860 slave schedule. The title chain is a bridge for property research; biological descent still requires its own evidence.

Helen Armstrong / Helen Gilbert

The 2006 foreclosure record is an additional independent primary-source confirmation that Helen Armstrong and Helen Gilbert are the same person. It joins the Nichols property chain to the later Armstrong family record.

Cause No. 97V-003 · 155th Judicial District Court of Austin County, Texas · recorded November 1, 2006 · John Nichols Survey Abstract No. 73 · ACAD Account No. R20014 · Austin County Deed Records Vol. 209 Page 228.

From Tennessee to Bellville
The timeline preserves the major documentary anchors without collapsing them into one family story.
1828–1829 · Tennessee

Harriet appears by name

The federal slave schedule records 24 enslaved people in the Nichols household in Williamson County.

1830 U.S. Federal Slave Schedule · Williamson County, Tennessee.
1832–1835 · Tennessee → Texas

Milley, Harriet & infant Fanny become a migration lead

Bedford's attachment sought Milley, Harriet, and Harriet's infant daughter Fanny. Nichols refused surrender; the sheriff later marked the return Not Found. Nichols was subsequently documented in Texas.

Bedford vs. Nichols · Williamson County Chancery Court · FamilySearch Image Group 008479344.

One unnamed “dependent”

The Stephen F. Austin Register of Families records John Nicholls, Fanny, two children, and one other dependent. The person's name, age, sex, and exact status are not recorded in that entry. The person remains an early enslavement-network research target.

Stephen F. Austin Register of Families · Page 80.

Mexican land grant

John Nichols received one league and one labor on October 20, 1832. Later land transfers became part of the Bellville property network.

John Nichols marries Fanny Waldrop

Fanny Waldrop's later property history connects the Nichols household to the Patience/Clarissa Waldrop network.

Austin County marriage record · October 14, 1837.

Nine enslaved people recorded

The schedule names none of them. Their demographic profiles are preserved above. Joseph remains a hypothesis for one of the two mulatto males; Rendy and Easter are not assigned.

1860 U.S. Federal Slave Schedule · Austin County, Texas · Bellville · John Nichols household.
March 3, 1864

John Nichols dies

His probate file has not been located in the Austin County courthouse index under the searched spelling variants. The missing probate record remains an active research gap.

Austin County Clerk correspondence · Stephanie Kovar · 2026.
June 19, 1865

Emancipation reaches Texas

The nine people recorded in 1860, if still held in the household in 1865, would have been among those freed under General Order No. 3. The later lives of the people are reconstructed separately rather than assumed.

General Order No. 3 · June 19, 1865.
1865–1869 · Bellville

Black Nichols families appear in the post-emancipation record

Joseph Nichols married Easter Bell after emancipation. Henry Nichols married Delia Manning in 1865 and Emeline Georgia in 1879. Joseph and James W. Nichols registered to vote in 1868.

1876–1879

Fanny's pension and the Nichols family's migration

Fanny Waldrop Nichols applied for a Texas Revolution widow's pension and lived in Travis County. Sam H. Nichols and James W. Nichols appear in the later pension correspondence from Travis and Coleman counties.

Texas Comptroller's Office Pension File · FamilySearch Image Group 008700661 · Images 482–496.
1930–1935 · Bellville

Later Nichols generations remain in Bellville

Emeline Nickols appears as a homeowner in 1930. Easter Bell Nichols died in Bellville in 1935. Their records demonstrate the longevity of the post-emancipation Nichols community, while individual links to the 1860 population remain under reconstruction.

2006 · Austin County

The Nichols Survey reappears through foreclosure

The tax foreclosure names a later group of Nichols descendants and heirs, including Easter Pink and Helen Armstrong/Helen Gilbert, preserving a long-range property and family network.

Cause No. 97V-003 · 155th Judicial District Court · Austin County Deed Records Vol. 209 Page 228.
12 / RENDY
Rendy Blayn · kept in the research, moved out of the schedule
Removing Rendy from the 1860 table does not remove the research lead.

Rendy Blayn remains a major research lead because Easter's 1935 death certificate names her mother. Easter's 1900 census gives her mother's birthplace as Arkansas; the 1910 census gives North Carolina. That discrepancy remains unresolved.

The Blain/Bland research includes a John Blain Class 3 headright in Fayette County, Texas, arriving between 1837 and 1840, and post-emancipation Bland/Blain families in the Bellville/Fayette County region. These records are leads toward Rendy's origin and migration, not proof that she was one of John Nichols's nine enslaved people.

This page therefore keeps the Rendy → Easter relationship visible while separating it from the John Nichols → nine unnamed people population until a documentary bridge is found.

13 / RESEARCH GAPS
What the archive is still looking for
The gaps are part of the evidence. They tell us exactly where the next search should go.
Identify the nine people in 1860
Search 1860–1870 Bellville records, Freedmen's Bureau Brenham subdistrict records, labor contracts, ration records, complaints, marriages, voter registrations, deeds, and later census households for age/sex/color combinations and relationships.
Test the Joseph hypothesis
Compare Joseph's known birth information with both mulatto male entries (age 22 and age 18), then look for a primary source that places Joseph in the Nichols household before emancipation.
Reconstruct the Patience / Clarissa cluster
Follow the 1790s–1839 South Carolina and Mississippi property records and connect Clarissa, Amanda, Harriet, and other descendants forward through Texas records without assuming they are identical to Rendy/Easter or the 1860 Nichols population.
Locate the missing John Nichols probate
The Austin County probate index search did not locate a file under the searched Nichols spelling variants. The probate gap remains significant because an estate inventory could potentially name enslaved people.
Follow the land chain
Review Austin County deed books 1837–1866, Spanish deed material from 1825–1835, and Volume 209 Page 228 to reconstruct how the Nichols Survey property moved through later families and heirs.
Search the Freedmen's Bureau
Austin County fell under the Brenham subdistrict. Labor contracts, rations, complaints, and other records from 1865–1870 may identify formerly enslaved members of the Nichols-area community by name.
14 / ARMSTRONG
Where the Nichols network reaches the Armstrong line
The Armstrong connection is preserved as a later family/community bridge, not used to backfill the 1860 identities.

Hellen/Helen Nichols Armstrong is part of the later Nichols family network and appears in the 2006 property/heir record as Helen Armstrong a.k.a. Helen Gilbert. Her daughter connects the Nichols line to the Armstrong family archive.

John Armstrong, who married Hellen Nichols Armstrong, was the son of Dave Armstrong, born in South Carolina, and Clara Morgan Armstrong, born in North Carolina ca. 1848. Dave and Clara married in Austin County on August 29, 1868 (marriage record No. 376). Death certificates for their daughter Ida Twiggs and mother Clara Armstrong list John Armstrong as informant and preserve the parents' birthplaces.

This is a community-network connection. It is not used to assign John Armstrong or his parents to a particular Nichols enslaved person without additional evidence.
